title: Type conversions and tests (is, as, typeof)
hook: Sometimes you need to turn one type into another or ask "what type is this?" C# gives you implicit conversions for safe changes, explicit casts for risky ones, and `is`/`as`/`typeof` for type questions.

blocks.text: A **conversion** changes a value from one type to another. **Implicit** conversions happen automatically when the compiler is sure no information is lost (`int` to `long`). **Explicit** casts (`(int)1.9`) can truncate or throw and require you to write the cast. **`is`** tests whether a value is compatible with a type and can introduce a new variable. **`as`** tries a reference conversion and returns `null` on failure. **`typeof`** gives you a `Type` object for a compile-time type name. **`GetType()`** returns the run-time type of an instance.

entries.plainDefinition: A conversion the compiler performs automatically because it is considered safe (widening numerics, upcasting references).
A conversion you write with parentheses. May truncate numbers or throw on failed reference casts.
Checks run-time type compatibility. Modern C# lets you write `if (msg is string body)` to test and bind in one step.
Returns a `System.Type` for a compile-time type name. Needs a type, not a variable: `typeof(string)`, not `typeof(myVar)`.

blocks.text: Auth payloads arrive as `object` or JSON. You must narrow them safely before use. A wrong cast throws `InvalidCastException` at run time. Comparing `GetType() == typeof(Base)` misses derived types — use `is` instead. Parsing CSV grades with `(int)double.Parse("3.7")` truncates to `3` instead of rounding — use `decimal` and explicit rounding rules.

blocks.title: Compile-time vs run-time
blocks.body: `typeof` and overload resolution are compile-time. `GetType()`, `is`, and virtual method dispatch use run-time type. `nameof` returns a string name — it is not a `Type` object.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Safe widening? → implicit
items.body: `int` to `long`, `float` to `double`, derived class to base class — no cast needed.

items.title: Narrowing or downcasting? → explicit cast
items.body: `(int)1.9` truncates. `(Derived)baseRef` throws if the object is not actually `Derived`.

items.title: Test without throwing? → is or as
items.body: `is` returns `bool` (and can bind a variable). `as` returns `null` on failure — only for reference and nullable types.

items.title: Need type metadata? → typeof or GetType
items.body: `typeof(AuthDto)` at compile time. `payload.GetType()` for the actual run-time type of this instance.

diagram.title: Conversion and type-test toolkit
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  W["Widening numeric"] -->|implicit| OK["No cast needed"]
  N["Narrowing numeric"] -->|"(int)"| TRUNC["May truncate"]
  UP["Base reference"] -->|implicit| SAFE["Safe upcast"]
  DOWN["Derived test"] -->|"is / as"| TEST["No throw on fail"]
  META["Type metadata"] --> TYPEOF["typeof — compile time"]
  META --> GETTYPE["GetType — run time"]

snippet.label: is and as with an auth payload
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `is string jwt` tests and binds in one step — no cast needed inside the block. Line 8: `as` returns `null` instead of throwing when the object is not `AuthDto`. Never use `as` on a non-nullable value type like `int`.

snippet.label: typeof vs GetType vs nameof
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `typeof` resolves at compile time — works with unbound generics too. Line 2: `GetType()` is virtual and returns the real run-time type (may be a subclass). Line 3: `nameof` is for identifier strings in refactor-safe code. Line 6: `typeof(payload)` does not compile.

snippet.label: Numeric casts truncate; checked catches overflow
snippet.explanation: Line 1: floating-to-integer cast truncates toward zero. Lines 4–5: unchecked narrowing may wrap; `checked` throws on overflow (see module 02). Line 7: parse grades as `decimal`, not `(int)double.Parse`.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `GetType() == typeof(Base)` and missing derived types — use `is` instead. Using `as` on `int` — it does not compile; use a nullable or a cast. Parsing CSV with `(int)double.Parse` and losing fractional grades — use `decimal` and explicit rounding.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: pattern matching with `is` avoids double lookup and null checks — prefer `if (obj is Derived d)` over `as` plus null test in new code. Failed reference casts throw InvalidCastException at run time; `as` returns null — choose based on whether failure is exceptional or expected. Narrowing numeric casts truncate toward zero — CSV grade import with `(int)3.9` becomes 3 silently; use explicit rounding policy. User-defined conversions (module 05) can hide cost — implicit conversions that allocate are a production footgun.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Silent null — easy to forget check

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using GetType() == typeof(Base) for polymorphism. Using as on int. Not knowing narrowing truncates instead of rounds. Saying as and cast are identical for value types.

interviewTakeaways: typeof is compile-time; GetType() is exact run-time type.
is pattern matching preferred over as + null check for reference types.
Narrowing numeric casts truncate toward zero — they do not round.
60s: is for safe test and bind. as returns null on fail — references only. Casts throw. GetType is exact, not polymorphic.
Follow-up: when does boxing happen during conversion to object?
commonPitfalls: as on value types — does not compile.
Strong answer: 'is pattern for polymorphism. as when null is expected. Narrowing truncates. GetType is exact type.'
Using `GetType() == typeof(Base)` and missing derived types — want `is`.
`as` on `int` — does not compile; use a nullable or a cast.
Parsing CSV with `(int)double.Parse` and losing fractional grades — use `decimal`.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `typeof` returns a string tag. C# `typeof` returns `System.Type`. JavaScript `instanceof` is closer to C# `is` for reference types.
